title: Promises and Async/Await
summary: A Promise is a contract that settles exactly once; async/await is sugar over that contract, not a new execution model. The four combinators differ entirely in how they treat rejection.

slides.markdown:
A Promise is a formal contract for a value you don't have yet: it starts **pending**, and settles to either **fulfilled** or **rejected** — exactly once, ever. Every API built on top — `.then` chaining, `Promise.all`, `async`/`await` — is built entirely on that one guarantee.

`async`/`await` doesn't replace Promises or introduce a new concurrency model; it's syntax that makes promise chains read like synchronous code, compiling down to the same [event-loop-and-async](event-loop-and-async) microtask mechanism underneath. Understanding Promises as a state machine, and `async`/`await` as sugar over it, is what turns "why did my loop run one request at a time" from a mystery into an obvious consequence.

slides.subTitle: Pending to fulfilled/rejected, exactly once
Return values, thrown errors, flattening
slides.markdown:
Each `.then` call returns a **new** Promise, which is what makes chaining work:

```javascript
fetchUser(id)
  .then((user) => fetchPosts(user.id))   // returning a Promise flattens automatically
  .then((posts) => posts.length)          // returning a plain value wraps it in a resolved Promise
  .then((count) => console.log(count))
  .catch((err) => console.error("failed:", err));
```

Three rules make this predictable: return a **plain value** from a `.then` callback, and the next `.then` receives it directly. Return **another Promise**, and the chain automatically "flattens" — it waits for that inner promise to settle before continuing, rather than handing the next `.then` a Promise-of-a-Promise. **Throw** (or return a rejected Promise), and the chain skips every following `.then` until it finds a `.catch`.

slides.subTitle: `all` vs `allSettled` vs `race` vs `any` — failure semantics
slides.markdown:
All four take an array of promises and return one promise. They differ entirely in how they treat rejection:

| | Resolves when | Rejects when |
|---|---|---|
| **`Promise.all`** | every input fulfills | **any single one** rejects — immediately, discarding the rest |
| **`Promise.allSettled`** | every input settles, fulfilled or rejected | never — always resolves with a per-item status/value or reason |
| **`Promise.race`** | the **first** input to settle, fulfilled or rejected | same — first settlement wins, win or lose |
| **`Promise.any`** | the **first** input to fulfill | only if **all** inputs reject |

`all` is "I need everything, and one failure ruins the batch." `allSettled` is "I need everything, and I want to know per-item what happened." `race` is "whoever answers first, good or bad." `any` is "whoever answers first with a *success*."

```javascript
const tasks = [fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]; // B rejects after 50ms, A and C take 500ms

Promise.all(tasks).catch((e) => console.log("all failed fast:", e));
Promise.allSettled(tasks).then((r) => console.log("allSettled waited:", r));
```

`Promise.all` rejects the instant `fetchB` rejects, around 50ms in — it doesn't wait for `fetchA`/`fetchC` to finish, even though they're still running in the background and will settle regardless. `Promise.allSettled` waits the full 500ms for every promise to settle, then resolves with an array describing each one's outcome individually.

slides.subTitle: What the transpiled version looks like
When parallel would do
Errors that vanish silently
slides.markdown:
A rejected Promise with **no** `.catch` (and not inside a `try`/`catch` around an `await`) doesn't crash your program the way a thrown synchronous error would — by default it can fail completely silently:

```javascript
async function risky() { throw new Error("boom"); }
risky(); // fire-and-forget — the rejection has no handler anywhere
```

In a browser, this fires an `unhandledrejection` event on `window` (visible in the console as a warning, easy to miss in a busy log); in Node, unhandled rejections crash the process by default in recent versions, but historically just warned. Either way, the practical danger is the same: a bug in an unawaited async call can fail with no visible symptom except "the thing that was supposed to happen didn't." The fix is disciplined: never call an `async` function or create a Promise without either `await`-ing it inside a `try`/`catch`, chaining a `.catch`, or explicitly deciding the rejection is safe to ignore.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance

slides.sectionTitle: Racing a request against a timeout

slides.markdown:
A senior answer to "how would you fetch these five things" names the actual failure semantics you want, not just "I'd use async/await":

- **All five required, any failure is fatal** → `Promise.all` (or sequential `await`s if one truly depends on another's result).
- **All five wanted, but partial results are still useful** → `Promise.allSettled`, then filter for the fulfilled ones.
- **Only the fastest answer matters, success or failure** → `Promise.race`.
- **Only the fastest *successful* answer matters** (e.g. querying redundant mirrors) → `Promise.any`.
- **A hard deadline on how long to wait** → `Promise.race` against a timer, ideally paired with `AbortController` to actually cancel the losing work.

Naming the combinator by its failure behavior, not its name, is what reads as fluency — "I want partial results even if some fail, so `allSettled`" beats "I'd use `allSettled`" every time.
